All of Adam's scanning has
inspired me to do some scanning of my own. I now only
have about a
fourth of a box from the Bob Fabris collection unscanned. I
found
another binder of the ZGRASS documentation. Most of it was
identical to the last
one, but I did find a more preliminary version of
the glossary.

The rest of it is from a big stack of unsorted
papers. There is a little bit of
everything here, so I won't go through
it all. Barry McCleave wrote a letter to
the editor detailing his
thoughts on a bank switched cartridge. There is a
draft of the
introduction Bob Fabris wrote for Bally Alley. George Moses tells
Bob
Fabris that Bob Weber has released all 45 W&W programs for publication
in
the Arcadian. Many of these were never actually printed, so we should
be on the
lookout for the source code of the last couple of unarchived
programs. There is
a bill of materials from Astrovision breaking down
the cost of every single
component of the system. There are instructions
and source code for Bowling
Secretary by New Image. Rich Tietjens wrote
a tutorial on random number
generation.

I've been
following Adam's lead and mostly scanning in grayscale. This does
go
much faster, because the scans are almost always of good
quality.

Paul

     Imagine controlling a coil spring inside of a building located in deep space. There is no gravity or friction to slow it down! Now imagine that you must avoid being hit by a battery of laser canons that keep shooting faster the longer you stay alive, and try to pick up valuable gold rings!

     This is how this fast paced game is played! "Turning it over" (12,500 points) will start your game over with the number of SPRINGS you have left plus one, which, by then, will be a welcome relief!!

     Options include:

     1 to 4 Players
     Individual selection of laser firing speeds
     Individual selection of the number of SPRING THINGS
     Individual selection of hand controls
     Continuous play or Stop after each SPRING

     This game can be played on ANY BLUE RAM BASIC!

All of Adam's scanning has
inspired me to do some scanning of my own. I now only
have about a
fourth of a box from the Bob Fabris collection unscanned. I
found
another binder of the ZGRASS documentation. Most of it was
identical to the last
one, but I did find a more preliminary version of
the glossary.

The rest of it is from a big stack of unsorted
papers. There is a little bit of
everything here, so I won't go through
it all. Barry McCleave wrote a letter to
the editor detailing his
thoughts on a bank switched cartridge. There is a
draft of the
introduction Bob Fabris wrote for Bally Alley. George Moses tells
Bob
Fabris that Bob Weber has released all 45 W&W programs for publication
in
the Arcadian. Many of these were never actually printed, so we should
be on the
lookout for the source code of the last couple of unarchived
programs. There is
a bill of materials from Astrovision breaking down
the cost of every single
component of the system. There are instructions
and source code for Bowling
Secretary by New Image. Rich Tietjens wrote
a tutorial on random number
generation.

I've been 
following Adam's lead and mostly scanning in grayscale. This does
go
much faster, because the scans are almost always of good
quality.

Here is a history of "Gobblers" which also includes documentation for the game:

"Gobblers"
By Bob Wiseman
ARCADIAN, 3, no. 12 (Oct. 5, 1981): 125. (Original Version)
ARCADIAN, 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1983): 56,70. (Klaus Doerge revision)
1983. (John J. Kottler revision)
Blue Ram BASIC, 2000-Baud, Requires Expansion RAM
Archived from Mike White Tape Collection.


This is a modified version of "Gobblers" by Bob Wiseman.  The most likely sequence of events for this modification is that Bob Wiseman wrote his original version of "Gobblers" in 1981.  Then Klaus Doerge modified "Gobbler" and had his mod published in the Arcadian in 1983.  After this, John J. Kottler modified Doerge's mod of "Gobblers" and Kottler's program eventually made its way into Mike White's collection.

Instructions for Gobblers (Original Version):

This is a two-player game played on a ten by five field.  The object of the game is to have your Gobbler gobble-up more squares than your opponent. When play begins, use the JX and JY to direct your Gobbler around the screen. Each printed square is worth one, two, three or four points depending upon how many dots are there.  The game ends when the last square is eaten.


Instructions for Gobblers (Klaus Doerge Revision):

This 2-player game requires you to eat a bunch of squares, where each square has one to four points in it, resulting in a score of 1 to 4 for each one eaten.  They are positioned in a 5 x 10 grid, and you utilize the JX and JY directions of your controller to move your man.  Of course, your opponent is doing the same.  The computer is keeping score.  It is listed in Bally BASIC,
but plays in AstroBASIC as well, just a bit faster.


Enjoy!

Adam

3)  GLEDBBAS.BIN - (Bally BASIC (Prototype) - Bally  4K) - This prototype of the original Bally BASIC was created by Richard Degler in March of 2010 using the Bally BASIC Demo cartridge.

6)  menu-demo.bin (Menu-Demo - Michael White  4K) - Demonstrates how to put graphics on the menu screen. This program is VERY short, but I've upload all 4K- almost all of it is empty space. Designed by Michael White.

7)  Music Decomposer (1983)(Richard Degler).bin (Music Decomposer - Richard Degler  4K) - Music Decomposer changes MUSIC STRINGS from cartridge format to AstroBASIC format.  This BASIC program is written for Blue Ram BASIC 1.1. The Music Decomposer binary works as a regular BASIC program, but it does NOT start as a cartridge. 8)  RAINBO2A.bin (Rainbow - Version 2 - Hanson  2K) - Rainbow (Ver. 2a) - By Hanson, with improvements from Richard Houser.  A program that puts a nice 66-color display on the screen

9)  Tester2 (Ken Lill)(2011)[8K Padded Version for EPROM].BIN - (Cartridge Tester - Ken Lill  8K) - This cartridge tester is used to test newly-created Bally/Astrocade cartridges. This cartridge requires expanded memory to run.

10) Words Of Wisdom (1979)(W&W Software Sales)[Tape to Cart Conversion - 2010].bin (Words of Wisdom - W&W Software Sales  8K) Ronaldo Goulart's 2010 BallyBASIC program to cart conversion.

11) XRAYMAZE (2010)(Bally)(Modified by Richard Degler).bin ( X-Ray Maze - Bally, Modified by Richard Degler  4K) - This is a modified version of Amazing Maze, VideoCade #5001 (in the Strategy series) for the Bally / Astrocade. 13) Yesterday (1986)(Richard Degler)(PD)(proto)[3'rd Version - Squelched (2008 Improvements)].bin (Part of "Beatles Music" archive)

"Gobblers"

 BASIC, 2000-Baud, Requires Expansion RAM
Archived from Mike White Tape Collection.


This is a modified version of "Gobblers" by Bob Wiseman.  The most likely sequence of events for this modification is that Bob Wiseman wrote his original version of "Gobblers" in 1981.  Then Klaus Doerge modified "Gobbler" and had his mod published in the Arcadian in 1983.  After this, John J. Kottler modified Doerge's mod of "Gobblers" and Kottler's program eventually made its way into Mike White's collection.

Instructions for Gobblers (Original Version):

This is a two-player game played on a ten by five field.  The object of the game is to have your Gobbler gobble-up more squares than your opponent. When play begins, use the JX and JY to direct your Gobbler around the screen. Each printed square is worth one, two, three or four points depending upon how many dots are there.  The game ends when the last square is
 eaten.


Instructions for Gobblers (Klaus Doerge Revision):

This 2-player game requires you to eat a bunch of squares, where each square has one to four points in it, resulting in a score of 1 to 4 for each one eaten.  They are positioned in a 5 x 10 grid, and you utilize the JX and JY directions of your controller to move your man.  Of course, your opponent is doing the same.  The computer is keeping score.  It is listed in Bally BASIC,
but plays in AstroBASIC as well, just a bit faster.


Enjoy!

Here is a history of "Gobblers" which also includes documentation for the game:

"Gobblers"
By Bob Wiseman
ARCADIAN, 3, no. 12 (Oct. 5, 1981): 125. (Original Version)
ARCADIAN, 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1983): 56,70. (Klaus Doerge revision)
1983. (John J. Kottler
 revision)
Blue Ram
 BASIC, 2000-Baud, Requires Expansion RAM
Archived from Mike White Tape Collection.


This is a modified version of "Gobblers" by Bob Wiseman.  The most likely sequence of events for this modification is that Bob Wiseman wrote his original version of "Gobblers" in 1981.  Then Klaus Doerge modified "Gobbler" and had his mod published in the Arcadian in 1983.  After this, John J. Kottler modified Doerge's mod of "Gobblers" and Kottler's program eventually made its way into Mike White's collection.

Instructions for Gobblers (Original Version):

This is a two-player game played on a ten by five field.  The object of the game is to have your Gobbler gobble-up more squares than your opponent. When play begins, use the JX and JY to direct your Gobbler around the screen. Each printed square is worth one, two, three or four points depending upon how many dots are there.  The game ends when the last square is
 eaten.


Instructions for Gobblers (Klaus Doerge Revision):

This 2-player game requires you to eat a bunch of squares, where each square has one to four points in it, resulting in a score of 1 to 4 for each one eaten.  They are positioned in a 5 x 10 grid, and you utilize the JX and JY directions of your controller to move your man.  Of course, your opponent is doing the same.  The computer is keeping score.  It is listed in Bally BASIC,
but plays in AstroBASIC as well, just a bit faster.


Enjoy!

Adam

Biorhythm Instructions:

This program displays the biorhythms of the user.  The program will request the birthday and the month to be displayed.  Up to 26 days are displayed at a time.  To see the next display use the "->" function.

The seven cycles are displayed separately by pressing their key.  On the display up is +, down is - and the center line can be brought in or out with its key.  There is also a moveable line to help line up particular days.  It is moved with KN(1) and is on until TR(1) is pulled.

The Cycles

* L - 13 Day - Health and Well Being
* S - 18 Day - Sexual Energies
  P - 23 Day - Physical, Strength, Endurance, Energy
  E - 28 Day - Emotions, Nerves, Feelings, Creativity
  I - 33 Day - Intelligence, Memory, Logic, Ambition
* C - 38 Day - Precognition, Premonition
* H - 43 Day - Natural High Cycle

* - Experimental Cycles Developed at NIU

The following instructions were typed from Mark Keller's original handwritten instructions that were included with the LISTing of the program.  These original instructions can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/mark_s_keller/Blackjack_II.pdf


"Blackjack II" Instructions:

This program implements the game of Blackjack for one player vs. the computer.  The rules are the same as those in the casinos with one exception.  The exception is that when you split your cards the dealer will play against each hand after you stand on it.  The stake you wish to play with is input from the keyboard at the start of the game.  The dealer alternates between two decks and only deals the top 26 cards from a deck.  Bets are entered from KN(1) [$1-$25 or $10-250 with the joystick pushed forward].

The commands from the joystick are:

STD = Stand
DBL - Double Down
SPL = Split

      STD
       ^
       |
SPL <-   -> DBL
       |
       V
      HIT

When the dealer's face-up card is an ACE, you may buy insurance, pull or push the joystick for a "YES."  All commands and bets are entered by pulling the trigger.

DELETE THE COMMENTS (.'S) to RUN!  [An alternate version of "Blackjack II" is included in the archive where Paul has removed the comments, so INPUT that version to actually play the game.]

The rest of the instructions contains a key with explanation to all the variables used in the program.

Dear Bob,

Here are the answers to your problems with my programs (I hope).  Lines 30-70
of Blockout 5.0 are:

50 CX=60;PRINT &2,L,
70 BOX C,-43,K,2,3;BOX Y,X,2,2,3

Yes, the line sequence in Pinball I goes 9, 10, 20, 40.

Both games ["Blockout" and "Pinball I"] were written as short, simple (and unfortunately slow) graphics games.

Blockout 5.0 is played like Breakout or Brickyard.  The game will prompt for parameters and hand controller &1 moves the paddle.

"Pinball I" is a simple pinball game (no gravity).  It will prompt for parameters, triggers 1 & 2 control the flippers.  They stay on a set period of time when used and then are disabled for a set period of time.  I'll send more game soon (I hope), and am now working on a Bally -> Vic-20 interface.

Mark

I have added seven Bally BASIC programs by Mark Keller to BallyAlley.com.  The instructions for all of these programs was hand-written.  I have typed it all in (minus Variable Lists).  Here is a list of the programs followed by a brief summary:

1) "Bombardment II 2.0" - This is a type of guessing game where the player pits his guesses against the computer's random choices. The player starts moving the cursor with the joystick and selecting his four "forts" with the trigger. The player and computer then alternate shots. The player shoots by moving the cursor on the computer's side to choose the "fort" to shoot at and then firing with the trigger. If the cursor stays lit it was a hit. The game restarts automatically.

2) "Bullseye II 2.0" - A dart game for up to 20 players. When 1-4 play, the game is pistol-grip controlled. When 5-20 play, keyboard input is used. The object of the game is to score 200 or more points. If more than 1 player score over 200 in 1 round, the highest score wins. There are three different throws.  There is no "best" or "worst" throw.

3) "Chase III 1.0" - In Chase, you are "*" in a high-voltage maze. There are robots "+" trying to destroy you. If you touch an "X", a "+", or are caught by a "+", you are destroyed. When the robots walk into "X"'s they are destroyed. The robots will follow the shortest route to you; allowing you to lead them to destruction.

4) "File Create" - This program is used to type in and record tape data files.

5) "Life" - Patterns are setup using the keys to move the cursor and turn it on and off. The game is then run. Generation and population counts are displayed. The game can be stopped and the pattern changed. The fate of a cell is defined by the number of cells neighboring it.
          
6) "Space Battle" - You have 50 time units to shoot down as many enemy space-craft as you can. The joystick controls your movement relative to the space-craft. The trigger fires the laser. Three misses are allowed per time period. The space-crafts movement becomes more evasive with each hit. Before you start the game by pulling the trigger, you can change the colors with the joystick.

7) "Star Trek III" - The play of this game is based loosely on Super Star Trek and Trek 80. You must destroy all Klingons before running out of energy or time.

"Tape Input/Output" Instructions:

This program is used to input a tape data file and then record copies of it when required.  To run the program, type:

GOSUB 200 <GO>

and enter the start and end @ index values.  Then type

:INPUT;RUN <GO>

and start the tape playing.  You can now HALT the program and inspect and change data, but don't change the program.  If you halted type:

GOTO 80 <GO>

Now in output mode, input start and end @ numbers for the recording, enter the NT (must be slow for some applications), start the tape recording and type GO to enter N

[Yes, the docs really end with "N" and no punctuation.]

The rest of the instructions contains a commented BASIC LISTing.

This is the only version of Text Editor that Paul Thacker found on tape, and he called it "Text Editor II" because that's what a comment in the code says. Lines 190-200 will print out the machine language data (for verification, he supposes). He's not sure why these lines weren't included in the printout.

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/mark_s_keller/TOC_Text_Editor_II.pdf

An earlier, all BASIC, version of the text editor ("Text Editor 5.0"), does NOT work 100% of the time and can mess up your program.  Note also that insert and delete are slow (because it doesn't use the machine language subroutines of "Text Editor II").  The BASIC listing and docs for "Text Editor 5.0" can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/mark_s_keller/Text_Editor_5.pdf


"Text Editor II" Instructions:

This is a text editor program that is placed at the beginning of your program.  It supports replacing, inserting and deleting.  Commands:

"ERASE" Key = Replace Character
      + Key = Insert Character
      - Key = Delete Character

Line 1 of "Text Editor II" is a comment that says:

1 .TEXT EDITOR II (to be replaced by a GOTO to program start)


Replace line 1 with a GOTO to your program.  Since RUN will cause the program to skip the editor, you must run "Text Editor II," with the following command:

GOTO 2 <GO>

When you run the "Text Edit" routine, enter the line number of the line to be changed.  Space through the line, changing what needs to be changed, and HALT when done editing.

Notes:

The machine language routines can be placed in the "Blue Ram unit."

The machine language routines are located at the following address locations:

Find   - $4EB0 (20144 decimal)
Delete - $4F1A (20250 decimal)
Insert - $4F2A (20266 in decimal)

The uncommented source code for the Find, Delete and Insert routines is
provided following the BASIC listing.

12802:
I added 15 Bally BASIC programs by Rich Tietjens.  The programs, with brief descriptions, are:

1) "23 Matches" (Alt. version) - Try to force the computer to take the last match."

2) "Alles Lookenspeepers" - Press any key to display letter written in a sort of German/English hybrid.

3) "Canary" - Plays a sound that resembles birdsong.

4. "Cash Register" - By John Eric, adapted by Rich Tietjens. Description of program from "Sourcebook" (Summer 1981), G-9, "A teaching game for ages 7-12. The program "buys" groceries and you must take change. A starter data file is supplied, along with a routine for you to make files."

5. "Craps" - This is a game for 1 to 4 players. when the title appears, press "1" to begin play. Press "0" to restore color, if the screen dims. When requested, enter the number of players, then press "GO".

6. "Fahrenheit Celsius Conversion" This program converts between Celsius and Fahrenheit or vice-versa.

7. "Hardcopy Converter" - This is a short utility to convert characters in a listing that may not work with a printer, such as changing the division sign to a forward slash. Version 2 of the program will automatically list the program when finished.

8. "Klingon Capture" - The Klingon Empire has violated the Organian Treat.  As Captain of the Enterprise, you must proceed immediately to Station K7 and capture a Klingon battle cruiser intact.

9. "Optical Density Map" by Rich Tietjens. Two versions are in the archive. One sorts the characters by ASCII value, and the other sorts the characters by density.  The LISTing describes itself as, "Optical density map of Bally printable characters for use in hard-copy psuedo-graphic printing." This information would be used to create images on a non-graphic printer.

10. "Sound Trek" - It's a space battle game played on an 8x8 grid, similar to MicroTrek. Comment from Sourcebook (Fall 1981): "'Sound Check' uses all available memory in the Arcade, including the keyboard and cassette buffers."

11. "Space War" (Proto) - Close with and destroy the enemy. Lasers are self-aiming but have limited range. Collision with the sun is fatal.  This game uses the hand controller to control your ship.  See archive for in-depth archiving explanation about this program.

12. "Star Trader" - This game is based on "Hamurabi" by Richard Houser, but with a space theme. Some garbage collects on the screen while the code loads, but it started fine, so this may be intended. If you earn too many credits that game will crash.

13. "Super Mastermind" - Super Mastermind lets you match wits with your Bally computer system. The computer will make a code sequence of five "colors." Each color will be represented by a number and you may choose to let the computer select from up to 9 numbers. You will have 12 turns to guess the sequence. After each turn, the computer will indicate how many numbers are in the correct position ("b" for black) and how many numbers are in the wrong position but are in the hidden code ("w" for white) when the program is ready, the title will appear on the screen.

14. "Touchtone Dialer, Directory"

The original version of this program, "Touchtone Simulate" by Chuck Thomka, appeared in Arcadian volume 1, page 65. Some modifications by Rich Tietjens were printed in Arcadian volume 2, page 90. This version is similar to that modified program, but not identical. It also includes a sample directory of phone numbers, and prints out instructions after the code loads.

15. "ZZZ-UNK-1st Line" - This unnamed program was named '1st Line' after some text in the code. It lists some code, but doesn't really do anything.

You can download the programs in the Rich Tietjens Bally BASIC Area:

http://tinyurl.com/2brgxud

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/Rich_Tietjens/Rich_Tietjens.html

Most of these programs have extra comments, so if you're interested in one in particular, then check the archive for more details.

I'll follow-up this posting with come comments on some of the programs that I find most interesting.

Enjoy!

1980
"Space Flight Package" Cassette

To Commander

     SFHQ

I went ahead and typed the code for "Standard Color Generator" into a hex editor (using WizHex), disassembled it (using dZ80 2.0), commented it (using PSPad), added some NOPs (so code is in the right place) and then assembled it (using Zmac).  The binary output is identical (save for the two NOPs that I added for spacing reasons).

The trouble is, THEN I read how "MLM" loads program data from tape using the *READ command.  I should have read this FIRST, for if I had done that, I may not have bothered with this test.  It seems that *READ loads quite differently from BASIC's :INPUT.

I expected the *READ command to work like this:

*READ 4EAD

In my eyes that would start loading byes at $4EAD (the beginning of "Standard Color Generator").  However, the command is much simpler-- but it probably won't seem so when I explain it here in a moment (we'll see...).

I'd like to know what an actual "MLM" program looks like by looking at the only archived MLM program.  Paul, could you please digitally archive "Goldfish Demo," here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/mlm_programs/Goldfish%20Demo%20(The%20Bit%20Fiddlers)(MLM).zip

I expect the text file that is created for "Goldfish Demo" to start off something like this:

[Decimal Memory Address]: [Data Byte][Decimal Memory Address]: [Data Byte]

For "Standard Color Generator," the first line of code is this (from the Source Listing):

4EAD  CD 47 23        CALL    CLEAR          ;  "MLM" "Clear [...]

I think that the code would look like this if loading $CD4723 (the first three bytes of the program) from tape:

4EAD3ACD204EAE3A47204EAF3A2320

It breaks down like this:

4EAD - Memory Address where program data will be stored
3A   - ASCII ":" = ADDR command
CD   - Program Data
20   - ASCII " " = WRITE command
4EAE - Memory Address
3A   - ASCII ":" = ADDR command
47   - Program Data
20   - ASCII " " = WRITE command
4EAF - Memory Address
3A   - ASCII ":" = ADDR command
23   - Program Data
20   - ASCII " " = WRITE command


This is what it would look like in those text files included with the archive programs:

"20141: 20520142: 7120143: 35 "

This seems wasteful as the data takes up more room than required.  However, this method does have the advantage that the code doesn't have to be contiguous.

In the meantime, following my signature, is the source code for "Standard Color Generator" which is then followed by the hex output (in ASCII format).  You can assemble it, but I'm not sure what you'll do with it yet, as a straight conversion of the binary output doesn't look like it will make a loadable program for "MLM."

Oh, and this is a nice diversion from uploading programs to the website... ;-)

Adam



;  "Standard Color Generator"
;  For Bally Arcade/Astrocade
;  By Andy Guevara
;  1982
;
;  This program generates 8 standard colors used in TV work.
;  
;  This assembly source code is from the "Machine Language Manager"
;  Manual, Page 7-4.
;
;  This program is for use with the 1982's "Machine Language Manager"
;  cartridge by The Bit Fiddlers.  The output of this program
;  must be loaded to a 300-baud "tape" and then loaded into the
;  "MLM" at memory address $4EAD:
;
;  This program can be assembled using the ZMAC assembler.  Type:
;
;      zmac -i -m -o STDColor.bin -x STDColor.lst STDColor.asm
;
;  Version History:
;    .01 (July 16, 2013) - First Distributed version. 
;                        - Assemly re-typed and commented by Adam Trionfo
;                        - This source has been kept as true to the
;                          original as possible, which is why it doesn't
;                          use HVGLIB.H and instead uses equates for
;                          CALLs to the ROM routines.

;  Equates

SYSTEM  EQU     $FF            ;  System CALL
SYSSUK  EQU     $FF            ;  System CALL with SUCK option ON
INTPC   EQU     $00            ;  #  0  ; INTerPret with Context create
EXIT    EQU     $02            ;  #  2  ; eXit INTerpreter with Context
SETOUT  EQU     $16            ;  # 22  ; Set Display Ports
COLSET  EQU     $18            ;  # 24  ; COLors SET
RECTAN  EQU     $1C            ;  # 28  ; paint a RECTANgle
CLEAR   EQU     $2347          ;  "MLM" "Clear Screen" Routine

        ORG     $4EAD          ; Start of Program              

        CALL    CLEAR          ;  "MLM" "Clear Screen" Routine
        DB      SYSSUK         ;  Start Interpreter with SUCK option ON
        DB      INTPC          ;  Begin Interpretering
        DB      SETOUT+1       ;  Set Display Ports 
        DB      $B6            ;  Blank Line = 182  (VERtical Blanking Line)
        DB      $13            ;  Right/Left Bounds (HORizontal Color Boundary)
        DB      $08            ;  Interrupt Line    (VERtical Blanking Line)
        ;
        DB      COLSET+1       ;  UPI COLors SET
        DW      L4EEB          ;  Color List
        DB      EXIT+1         ;  Stop Interpreter        
        LD      BC,$486E       ;  White Border
        LD      A,$55          ;  Color #1
        LD      DE,$0614
        DB      SYSTEM         ;  Start Interpreter 
        DB      RECTAN         ;  On-Board ROM Routine - Paint a Rectangle
        LD      HL,L4EDA       ;  Table Address
        LD      D,$09          ;  Y Postion of Bars          
        LD      B,$08          ;  # of Bars
L4ECB:  PUSH    BC             ;  Save it
        LD      A,(HL)         ;  Get Colors from Table
        INC     HL
        LD      E,(HL)         ;  Get X Position
        INC     HL
        LD      BC,$420E       ;  Bar Size
        DB      SYSTEM         ;  Begin UPI Interpreting 
        DB      RECTAN         ;  On-Board ROM Routine - Paint a Rectangle
        POP     BC             ;  Get Back Count
        DJNZ    L4ECB          ;  Loop Back
        RET                    ;  All Done

        NOP                    ;  Filler Byte (So Data is Contiguous on Tape)

;  Table
L4EDA:  DB      $00,$17        ;  Color 00, at X=$17
        DB      $55,$24
        DB      $AA,$33
        DB      $FF,$3F
        DB      $00,$4C
        DB      $55,$57
        DB      $AA,$64
        DB      $FF,$71

        NOP                    ;  Filler Byte (So Data is Contiguous on Tape)

;  Color List
L4EEB:  DB      $AC            ; Green---+
        DB      $86            ; Yellow--+-- Left Colors
        DB      $07            ; White   |
        DB      $00            ; Black---+
;
        DB      $CD            ; Cyan----+
        DB      $5A            ; Red     +-- Right Colors
        DB      $2B            ; Magenta |
        DB      $F9            ; Blue----+

END                            ; End of Program

12811:
A quick and dirty way to load the "Standard Color Generator" program into the "MLM" would be to do this:

1) Convert the "Standard Color Generator's" hex file using the method that works for Bally BASIC.

2) Using Bally BASIC, load "Standard Color Generator" into the expanded memory area at $6000.

3) Write protect RAM and take out the Bally BASIC cart and put in the "MLM" cart.

4) Use the System ROM's MOVE command to move the program from expanded memory to screen RAM.  Here the 9-byte program I just "wrote" (if you can call it that) to do this:

        DB      $FF       ; SYSTEM
        DB      $5E       ; System ROM CALL - MOVE block transfer
        DW      $4EAD     ; Destination
        DW      $0044     ; 68 Program Bytes to Move
        DW      $6000     ; Source of Program
        RET

Here's the binary output of this program:

FF5EAD4E44000060C9

The program is relocatable, so it can be placed anywhere.  It will probably fit at $4Ef3 (the bytes immediately after "Standard Color Generator," after it's been moved).  Unless the "MLM" cart is using those nine bytes from $4EF3-$4EFB, then there shouldn't be a problem.

After the MOVE program is run, then the "Standard Color Generator" program will be in the MLM's" RAM and can be SAVED to tape using "MLM's" *WRITE command.

Is this convoluted?  Sure... but it seems like it will work and it isn't much more difficult then some of the other methods of archiving that Paul has used already for some unusual programs.

Anyway, that's just a thought.

The MOVE routine I just posted for use with "MLM" uses three sets of registers: DE, HL and BC.  So I think that those would have to be pushed onto the stack and then popped off (unless the routine already does it... I doubt it).  If the routine doesn't do it, then this will work:

        PUSH    DE
        PUSH    HL
        PUSH    BC
        DB      $FF       ; SYSTEM
        DB      $5E       ; System ROM CALL - MOVE block transfer
        DW      $4EAD     ; Destination
        DW      $0044     ; 68 Program Bytes to Move
        DW      $6000     ; Source of Program
        POP     BC
        POP     HL
        POP     DE
        RET

The 15 byte program would look like this:

D5E5C5FF5EAD4E44000060C1E1D1C9

If you assembly the above program with Zmac, then it will be easier to read the individual bytes needed to input the program.

Hopefully this method isn't needed to load or save "Standard Color Generator" with MLM, but it's nice to know that the option is available in a pinch.

If all else fails, then the program can always be input straight into MLM.  But where's the fun in that?

Adam

        DB      SETOUT+1       ;  Set Display Ports 
        DB      $B6            ;  Blank Line = 182  (VERtical Blanking Line)
        DB      $13            ;  Right/Left Bounds (HORizontal Color Boundary)

Here are the full instructions, which I OCR'ed and proofread today:

FLYING ACE Game instructions:

Using hand control #1, turn the knob until the desired number of players is shown on screen. Pull the trigger and play begins.

Hand control functions are:

TRIGGER  - Fires at enemy bi-plane

JOYSTICK - Controls flight of your airplane flight. Back on the handle makes you go up and the enemy goes down. Left makes you fly left but the enemy moves right.

KNOB - Inputs number of players and has no function during game play.


PLAYING THE GAME

Your turn is noted when your player number (Top of screen) is blacked out. Quickly try to maneuver the enemy into your gun sight and fire. Your shots are limited and so is your time. The more you shoot the more time is used. If you can get the enemy within the first few seconds or shots you will be awarded a bonus turn and get to shoot again right away.

Flying your plane is the most tricky part of this game. If the enemy is to your right, move the joystick toward the right. This sounds easy but it takes some practice. Also note that if the bi-plane sound is getting higher then he is diving. If the sound is getting lower then that means he is going up. If he banks to the right he is moving right, banking left, he is going left. If he is level, he is going straight ahead but he may be going up or down at the same time.

If you run out of time you will hear a high pitch beeping meaning you have only about 2 shots or 4 seconds to shoot the enemy. If you fail you are zapped and a large "ZAP" or "POW" will appear in you gun sight window, play goes on to the next player.

SCORING

Up to 250 points are possible for a quickly shot down enemy.

As time goes on and for each miss points are deducted.

12822:
To get my mind off of other things going on right now, I've been messing about with my on-again/off-again disassembly of "The Incredible Wizard."  I've managed to find pretty-much all of the graphics.  These graphics range from $36D6-$3A04 and take up about 800 bytes of ROM space.  It might not sound like much, but that's about half the size of some of the smaller Astrocade ROM carts, so it's quite a significant jump.

I'm currently working on figuring out the sound data.  Most carts for the Astrocade use MUSIC subroutines located in the on-board ROM for sound effects.  So far, I haven't run into these routines at all.  I certainly have run into WOW's own routines though.  I'm not sure why these routines were used instead of the on-board routines.  Maybe to get a greater range of sounds and more control.  It certainly would be cool if it was because the original sound effects from the arcade game were ripped for the home version.  I have no way of knowing that right now-- and somehow I doubt it.

Figuring-out the data for the sound effects is slow going, but it's pretty neat and I'm learning about the sound synthesizer, as I have to keep referencing the HVGLIB header file.  In order to get all the sound data labeled I'm going to have to really start digging into the sound routines, which will be time consuming.  For now, I'm just fitting this disassembly in here and there.

Eventually I may look for the routines that draw the levels.  I thought that they'd be easy to spot, but they are not.

Adam

To get my mind off of other things going on right now, I've been messing about with my on-again/off-again disassembly of "The Incredible Wizard."  I've managed to find pretty-much all of the graphics.  These graphics range from $36D6-$3A04 and take up about 800 bytes of ROM space.  It might not sound like much, but that's about half the size of some of the smaller Astrocade ROM carts, so it's quite a significant jump.


I'm currently working on figuring out the sound data.  Most carts for the Astrocade use MUSIC subroutines located in the on-board ROM for sound effects.  So far, I haven't run into these routines at all.  I certainly have run into WOW's own routines though.  I'm not sure why these routines were used instead of the on-board routines.  Maybe to get a greater range of sounds and more control.  It certainly would be cool if it was because the original sound effects from the arcade game were ripped for the home version.  I have no way of knowing that right now-- and somehow I doubt it.


Figuring-out the data for the sound effects is slow going, but it's pretty neat and I'm learning about the sound synthesizer, as I have to keep referencing the HVGLIB header file.  In order to get all the sound data labeled I'm going to have to really start digging into the sound routines, which will be time consuming.  For now, I'm just fitting this disassembly in here and there.


Eventually I may look for the routines that draw the levels.  I thought that they'd be easy to spot, but they are not.

Adam

12839:
OK, I spent some more time with the Machine Language Manager today. After reading enough of the instruction manual to figure out how to actually enter and run programs, I entered the ASCII Character Generator hex code. I saved it to tape (well, my PC) by entering:

*[WRITE]4F30[ADDR]4F3B[LIST]

I'm denoting keywords in brackets here.

When I processed the recording and converted it to a text file, I got this.

4F30:4F3B
4F30: CD 05 24 06 3B 3E 20 D7
4F38: 3C 10 FC C9 FF FF FF FF

This is much simpler than the Goldfish example, maybe in part because it doesn't autostart. The entire program is stored in the Bally BASIC character set, even though it's only using 18 characters here--the hex values 0-F, a colon, and a space. It automatically divided into eight bytes per line, with the address at the start of each line. It filled out the final line with FF even though I didn't tell it to list this far.

Pressing reset when using the Machine Language Manager doesn't actually clear the memory, so I turned my system off and on, then loaded and ran the processed recording with:

*[READ]{Play the recording to completion and it prints on screen.}
**4F30[CALL]

It does indeed print out the Machine Language Manager character set.

I next took Adam's text version of the Standard Color Generator program and tried to format it like this. At first my addresses were off, because I didn't realize initially that it was leaving a little space between the code, the table, and the color list. So, I couldn't put eight bytes on every line, and I wasn't sure if I should put the address range at the top. I ended up just trying the following as the .txt file, and it worked fine, displaying a color pattern on the TV when run as before, except calling the starting address of 4EAD.

4EAD: CD 47 23 FF 00 17 B6 13
4EB5: 08 19 EB 4E 03 01 6E 48
4EBD: 3E 55 11 14 06 FF 1C 21
4EC5: DA 4E 16 09 06 08 C5 7E
4ECD: 23 5E 23 01 0E 42 FF 1C
4ED5: C1 10 F3 C9
4EDA: 00 17 55 24 AA 33 FF 3F
4EE2: 00 4C 55 57 AA 64 FF 71
4EEB: AC 86 07 00 CD 5A 2B F9

As far as I can tell, the same technique should work for the other example programs in the manual--Critter and 256 Color Program. Are there any other Machine Language Manager programs available?

I'll send Adam the files I discussed.

Paul

> ;  "Standard Color Generator"
>
> ;  For Bally Arcade/Astrocade
> 
> ;  By Andy Guevara
>
> ;  1982
>
> ;
>
> ;  This program generates 8 standard colors used in TV work.
>
> ;
>
> ;  This assembly source code is from the "Machine Language Manager"
>
> ;  Manual, Page 7-4.
>
> ;
>
> ;  This program is for use with the 1982's "Machine Language Manager"
>
> ;  cartridge by The Bit Fiddlers.  The output of this program
>
> ;  must be loaded to a 300-baud "tape" and then loaded into the
>
> ;  "MLM" at memory address $4EAD:
>
> ;
>
> ;  This program can be assembled using the ZMAC assembler.  Type:
>
> ;
>
> ;      zmac -i -m -o STDColor.bin -x STDColor.lst STDColor.asm
>
> ;
>
> ;  Version History:
>
> ;    .01 (July 16, 2013) - First Distributed version.
>
> ;                        - Assemly re-typed and commented by Adam Trionfo
>
> ;                        - This source has been kept as true to the
>
> ;                          original as possible, which is why it doesn't
>
> ;                          use HVGLIB.H and instead uses equates for
>
> ;                          CALLs to the ROM routines.
>
>
>
> ;  Equates
>
>
>
> SYSTEM  EQU     $FF            ;  System CALL
>
> SYSSUK  EQU     $FF            ;  System CALL with SUCK option ON
>
> INTPC   EQU     $00            ;  #  0  ; INTerPret with Context create
>
> EXIT    EQU     $02            ;  #  2  ; eXit INTerpreter with Context
>
> SETOUT  EQU     $16            ;  # 22  ; Set Display Ports
>
> COLSET  EQU     $18            ;  # 24  ; COLors SET
>
> RECTAN  EQU     $1C            ;  # 28  ; paint a RECTANgle
>
> CLEAR   EQU     $2347          ;  "MLM" "Clear Screen" Routine
>
>
>
>         ORG     $4EAD          ; Start of Program
>
> 
>
>         CALL    CLEAR          ;  "MLM" "Clear Screen" Routine
>
>         DB      SYSSUK         ;  Start Interpreter with SUCK option ON
>
>         DB      INTPC          ;  Begin Interpretering
>
>         DB      SETOUT+1       ;  Set Display Ports
>
>         DB      $B6            ;  Blank Line = 182  (VERtical Blanking Line)
>
>         DB      $13            ;  Right/Left Bounds (HORizontal Color Boundary)
>
>         DB      $08            ;  Interrupt Line    (VERtical Blanking Line)
>
>         ;
>
>         DB      COLSET+1       ;  UPI COLors SET
>
>         DW      L4EEB          ;  Color List
>
>         DB      EXIT+1         ;  Stop Interpreter
>
>         LD      BC,$486E       ;  White Border
>
>         LD      A,$55          ;  Color #1
>
>         LD      DE,$0614
>
>         DB      SYSTEM         ;  Start Interpreter
>
>         DB      RECTAN         ;  On-Board ROM Routine - Paint a Rectangle
>
>         LD      HL,L4EDA       ;  Table Address
>
>         LD      D,$09          ;  Y Postion of Bars
>
>         LD      B,$08          ;  # of Bars
>
> L4ECB:  PUSH    BC             ;  Save it
>
>         LD      A,(HL)         ;  Get Colors from Table
>
>         INC     HL
>
>         LD      E,(HL)         ;  Get X Position
>
>         INC     HL
>
>         LD      BC,$420E       ;  Bar Size
>
>         DB      SYSTEM         ;  Begin UPI Interpreting
>
>         DB      RECTAN         ;  On-Board ROM Routine - Paint a Rectangle
>
>         POP     BC             ;  Get Back Count
>
>         DJNZ    L4ECB          ;  Loop Back
>
>         RET                    ;  All Done
>
>
>
>         NOP                    ;  Filler Byte (So Data is Contiguous on Tape)
>
>
>
> ;  Table
>
> L4EDA:  DB      $00,$17        ;  Color 00, at X=$17
>
>         DB      $55,$24
>
>         DB      $AA,$33
>
>         DB      $FF,$3F
>
>         DB      $00,$4C
>
>         DB      $55,$57
>
>         DB      $AA,$64
>
>         DB      $FF,$71
>
>
>
>         NOP                    ;  Filler Byte (So Data is Contiguous on Tape)
>
>
>
> ;  Color List
>
> L4EEB:  DB      $AC            ; Green---+
>
>         DB      $86            ; Yellow--+-- Left Colors
>
>         DB      $07            ; White   |
>
>         DB      $00            ; Black---+
>
> ;
>
>         DB      $CD            ; Cyan----+
>
>         DB      $5A            ; Red     +-- Right Colors
>
>         DB      $2B            ; Magenta |
>
>         DB      $F9            ; Blue----+
>

>

If pressing reset cleared memory than it would truly be a pain to enter and test machine language programs.  It's not uncommon for a ML program to enter never-never land.  In BASIC you can press HALT.  Without that HALT option in MLM, then the only chance to gain control of the system again is with Reset. probably would have done better than it did in 1982/83.   In 1978 more people would
have played around with machine language since BASIC wasn't included
with the original Arcade.  In 1978 there were plenty of people that used BASIC just as a means to enter machine language programs.  If MLM had been available from the beginning of the Bally Arcade's lifespan, then I'm sure that some early adapters would have preferred the MLM over the BASIC cartridge.       OK, I spent some more time with the Machine Language Manager today. After reading enough of the instruction manual to figure out how to actually enter and run programs, I entered the ASCII Character Generator hex code. I saved it to tape (well, my PC) by entering:



*[WRITE]4F30[ADDR]4F3B[LIST]



I'm denoting keywords in brackets here.



When I processed the recording and converted it to a text file, I got this.



4F30:4F3B

4F30: CD 05 24 06 3B 3E 20 D7

4F38: 3C 10 FC C9 FF FF FF FF



This is much simpler than the Goldfish example, maybe in part because it doesn't autostart. The entire program is stored in the Bally BASIC character set, even though it's only using 18 characters here--the hex values 0-F, a colon, and a space. It automatically divided into eight bytes per line, with the address at the start of each line. It filled out the final line with FF even though I didn't tell it to list this far.



Pressing reset when using the Machine Language Manager doesn't actually clear the memory, so I turned my system off and on, then loaded and ran the processed recording with:



*[READ]{Play the recording to completion and it prints on screen.}

**4F30[CALL]



It does indeed print out the Machine Language Manager character set.



I next took Adam's text version of the Standard Color Generator program and tried to format it like this. At first my addresses were off, because I didn't realize initially that it was leaving a little space between the code, the table, and the color list. So, I couldn't put eight bytes on every line, and I wasn't sure if I should put the address range at the top. I ended up just trying the following as the .txt file, and it worked fine, displaying a color pattern on the TV when run as before, except calling the starting address of 4EAD.



4EAD: CD 47 23 FF 00 17 B6 13

4EB5: 08 19 EB 4E 03 01 6E 48

4EBD: 3E 55 11 14 06 FF 1C 21

4EC5: DA 4E 16 09 06 08 C5 7E

4ECD: 23 5E 23 01 0E 42 FF 1C

4ED5: C1 10 F3 C9

4EDA: 00 17 55 24 AA 33 FF 3F

4EE2: 00 4C 55 57 AA 64 FF 71

4EEB: AC 86 07 00 CD 5A 2B F9



As far as I can tell, the same technique should work for the other example programs in the manual--Critter and 256 Color Program. Are there any other Machine Language Manager programs available?

Paul

> ;  For Bally Arcade/Astrocade

>

> ;  By Andy Guevara

>

> ;  1982

>

> ;

>

> ;  This program generates 8 standard colors used in TV work.

>

> ;

>

> ;  This assembly source code is from the "Machine Language Manager"

>

> ;  Manual, Page 7-4.

>

> ;

>

> ;  This program is for use with the 1982's "Machine Language Manager"

>

> ;  cartridge by The Bit Fiddlers.  The output of this program

>

> ;  must be loaded to a 300-baud "tape" and then loaded into the

>

> ;  "MLM" at memory address $4EAD:

>

> ;

>

> ;  This program can be assembled using the ZMAC assembler.  Type:

>

> ;

>

> ;      zmac -i -m -o STDColor.bin -x STDColor.lst STDColor.asm

>

> ;

>

> ;  Version History:

>

> ;    .01 (July 16, 2013) - First Distributed version.

>

> ;                        - Assemly re-typed and commented by Adam Trionfo

>

> ;                        - This source has been kept as true to the

>

> ;                          original as possible, which is why it doesn't

>

> ;                          use HVGLIB.H and instead uses equates for

>

> ;                          CALLs to the ROM routines.

>

>

>

> ;  Equates

>

>

>

> SYSTEM  EQU     $FF            ;  System CALL

>

> SYSSUK  EQU     $FF            ;  System CALL with SUCK option ON

>

> INTPC   EQU     $00            ;  #  0  ; INTerPret with Context create

>

> EXIT    EQU     $02            ;  #  2  ; eXit INTerpreter with Context

> 

> SETOUT  EQU     $16            ;  # 22  ; Set Display Ports

>

> COLSET  EQU     $18            ;  # 24  ; COLors SET

>

> RECTAN  EQU     $1C            ;  # 28  ; paint a RECTANgle

>

> CLEAR   EQU     $2347          ;  "MLM" "Clear Screen" Routine

>

>

>

>         ORG     $4EAD          ; Start of Program

>

>

>

>         CALL    CLEAR          ;  "MLM" "Clear Screen" Routine

>

>         DB      SYSSUK         ;  Start Interpreter with SUCK option ON

>

>         DB      INTPC          ;  Begin Interpretering

>

>         DB      SETOUT+1       ;  Set Display Ports

>

>         DB      $B6            ;  Blank Line = 182  (VERtical Blanking Line)

>

>         DB      $13            ;  Right/Left Bounds (HORizontal Color Boundary)

>

>         DB      $08            ;  Interrupt Line    (VERtical Blanking Line)

>

>         ;

> 

>         DB      COLSET+1       ;  UPI COLors SET

>

>         DW      L4EEB          ;  Color List

>

>         DB      EXIT+1         ;  Stop Interpreter

>

>         LD      BC,$486E       ;  White Border

>

>         LD      A,$55          ;  Color #1

>

>         LD      DE,$0614

>

>         DB      SYSTEM         ;  Start Interpreter

>

>         DB      RECTAN         ;  On-Board ROM Routine - Paint a Rectangle

>

>         LD      HL,L4EDA       ;  Table Address

>

>         LD      D,$09          ;  Y Postion of Bars

>

>         LD      B,$08          ;  # of Bars

>

> L4ECB:  PUSH    BC             ;  Save it

>

>         LD      A,(HL)         ;  Get Colors from Table

>

>         INC     HL

>

>         LD      E,(HL)         ;  Get X Position

> 

>         INC     HL

>

>         LD      BC,$420E       ;  Bar Size

>

>         DB      SYSTEM         ;  Begin UPI Interpreting

>

>         DB      RECTAN         ;  On-Board ROM Routine - Paint a Rectangle

>

>         POP     BC             ;  Get Back Count

>

>         DJNZ    L4ECB          ;  Loop Back

>

>         RET                    ;  All Done

>

>

>

>         NOP                    ;  Filler Byte (So Data is Contiguous on Tape)

>

>

>

> ;  Table

>

> L4EDA:  DB      $00,$17        ;  Color 00, at X=$17

>

>         DB      $55,$24

>

>         DB      $AA,$33

>

>         DB      $FF,$3F

>

>         DB      $00,$4C

>

>         DB      $55,$57

>

>         DB      $AA,$64

>

>         DB      $FF,$71

>

>

>

>         NOP                    ;  Filler Byte (So Data is Contiguous on Tape)

>

>

>

> ;  Color List

>

> L4EEB:  DB      $AC            ; Green---+

>

>         DB      $86            ; Yellow--+-- Left Colors

>

>         DB      $07            ; White   |

>

>         DB      $00            ; Black---+

>

> ;

>

>         DB      $CD            ; Cyan----+

>

>         DB      $5A            ; Red     +-- Right Colors

>

>         DB      $2B            ; Magenta |

>

>         DB      $F9            ; Blue----+

>

>

>

> END                            ; End of Program

>

>

>

12851:
I have added a disassembly of Spectre Systems' "ICBM Attack."  This source code assembles EXACTLY, byte for byte, into the "ICBM Attack" cart cartridge; there are no differences.

This game was designed and programmed by Brett Bilbrey.  Sound is by Marion Nelepa.  "ICBM Attack" requires a special analog hand controller to play - it can not be played without it.

After I uploaded my partial disassembly of "Wizard of Wor" on July 26'th I cleaned out my disassembly directory.  I came across a partially started disassembly of "ICBM Attack" that I began on November 18, 2011.  The only reason that I know the date I start it is because I put some comments in the disassembly.  Honestly, I just barely remember starting the disassembly.  There is a flicker in my mind that I was looking for SOMETHING in particular at the time, but I now forget what it was.  Rather than let what I'd started sit around unused on my hard drive (it was too much done to delete and too little to upload to the website), I thought that I'd clean it up.  I spent several hours with it over the last couple of days and the results are now available for download here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/icbm.asm

Most areas of the program have been identified as code or graphics.  If it's code, then it's been disassembled. If it's graphics, then it has been commented.  Most of the program still needs extensive comments, but it's got a surprising amount of progress made for the small amount of time that I've put into it (maybe twelve hours total-- and technically that's spread out over a couple of years).  This is the point where I'd have to dive into the program and start to follow the code much more.  For me, that means getting out a pencil and paper and working with the MESS debugger to see what's going on.  I don't have time for that... and there's really no reason to do it.

Maybe someone will take the disassembly and change it so that "ICBM Attack" uses the regular controller.  I wouldn't do that, as the game really would probably play poorly, but at least it would be playable on a real machine.  Sure Mike White hacked the program back in the 80's to use the regular controller, but it uses a combination of the Knob and Joystick-- it's quite hard to get used to using the hacked version.  Brett made the right choice by making this "ICBM Attack" use an analog controller.  It's just too bad that none of those controllers seem to be available anymore.  At least the game can still be played in MESS (and, it plays quite well, actually).

Have fun!

Adam

12863:
Longer answer on the "chicken.bin", a.k.a. in TOSEC: "Chicken (1986)(The
Bit Fiddlers and Mike White).bin", Cartridge image game - MESS v.0.140
and above no longer default the control ports to anything other than all
zeros.

Real hardware also doesn't clear the Screen RAM to zeros automatically
either, as you can see when you first turn one on before pressing RESET,
but this is not a problem here.

Not sure how this worked on a real Astrocade - without at least turning
it on to the Menu Screen to set the &(9) "Screen Split" port properly -
before inserting the cartridge, which never sets it.

The 2000-baud (and presumably the missing 300-baud) Basic tape program
would have set this before running the first load for the title screen,
and then loaded the machine code next.  But when that second load was
ripped out for a cartridge, the new loader code did not anticipate this.
Since Basic is not used in this 2K hack, it can not be called a
BasiCart...

So, what does the actual game look like before it is run?  Mostly a MLM
screen with a thin bar of a previously played game, followed by 1448
bytes of actual code and leftover system stack, as seen here or moved
elsewhere on the page:

  [Chicken! ROM Title screen]

>>
 I don't recall if we ever determined for certain that this was a

>>

I'm pretty sure that light pen interrupts ARE the problem.  Some of my "homebrew" programs broke, and they're still online in that condition!  Richard pointed out that it's because I was setting up the Astrocade for Light Pen interrupts, but that not handling them.  It didn't matter when MESS was ignoring them, but when it WASN'T ignoring light pen interrupts anymore, and I wasn't handling them in my program my program, then my program crashed.  One such program of mine, among others, is "8colors."  I set up my interrupt mod with:

        DB     $18        ; Interrupt Mode

Without consulting the Nutting Manual, I'm pretty sure the fix is just:

        DB     $08        ; Interrupt Mode

Any of the other programs, such as "Color Picker" just need this fixed too.  I can look into this more this week if anyone's interested.

12898:
The current name of the "Chicken!" ROM in the Astrocade ROM set is:

Chicken (1986)(The Bit Fiddlers and Mike White).bin

This name, like others other TOSEC names in the tape areas, doesn't reflect the true nature of the source material nor does it give a description of what is different.  The game is not a collaboration between The Bit Fiddlers and Mike White, but rather a later revision, which would today be considered a "hack."

Following the TOSEC standard, this version should be renamed to something like:

Chicken! (1982)(The Bit Fiddlers)(h Mike White)[1986 Cart Mod].bin

I THINK that this about covers what would be included in the name.  The explanation mark is allowed under the TOSEC rules, so the name is valid.  Here's a quick explanation of added changes:

(h Mike White) = Hack by Mike White
[1986 Cart Mod] = Cart mod created in 1986

How does this new name strike you, Paul?

Adam

Chicken (1986)(The Bit Fiddlers and Mike White).bin

This name, like others other TOSEC names in the tape areas, doesn't reflect the true nature of the source material nor does it give a description of what is different.  The game is not a collaboration between The Bit Fiddlers and Mike White, but rather a later revision, which would today be considered a "hack."

Following the TOSEC standard, this version should be renamed to something like:

Chicken! (1982)(The Bit Fiddlers)(h Mike White)[1986 Cart Mod].bin

(h Mike White) = Hack by Mike White

12938:
OK guys. Here's the scoop on the various Data Chips.
The original one was the one pictured - gray & white. The white area is the ceramic substrate. the gray areas are actually silver conductors. They were masked onto the white substrate and then ultra-fine wires connected the circuitry (under the black center area). The pins and their mounts were plated with industrial gold, .0063mils thick (some were .005 mils thick. Yes, they were extremely expensive. Not only for their precious metals, but for the fact thaty the processes for making those chips was still in it's infancy. Makink an individual mask (1 for each part number times the number of layers needed for the transistors and their interconnections). Their first yields were not that good. as they learned more and used better equipment, they improved and costs started to go down. Somewhere around 1978 the LSI (Large Scale Integration) chips began to standardize and the were able to change packaging. The silver was no longer needed as they used a metal
 framework that was similar in design to the silver's design, but then they were able to cover it in ceramic and later plastic. The pins were made into the framework, thus saving on cost for the gold and tooling and masks.
As for the metal bar used as a heatsink, the reason it gets hot is that it is drawing the heat away from the chip. The units made by Astrocade never had any heat sinks unless they were in the original batch from Bally. And they actually worked better. There were some improvements in the supporting circuitry to make the heat slightly less.
As far as the bar, it should be fine to use, as long as the bottom air vents don't blocked. The whole system is called a "chimney effect" type of cooling. The topmost area will have the most heat because heat rises. As that happens, it creates a vacuum underneath it, so it draws in the cooler air from the bottom.
Any Questions????

From the only guy that is currently repairing Bally/Astrocade units.
Ken

> OK guys. Here's the scoop on the various Data Chips.
> The original one was the one pictured - gray & white. The white area is the ceramic substrate. the gray areas are actually silver conductors. They were masked onto the white substrate and then ultra-fine wires connected the circuitry (under the black center area). The pins and their mounts were plated with industrial gold, .0063mils thick (some were .005 mils thick. Yes, they were extremely expensive. Not only for their precious metals, but for the fact thaty the processes for making those chips was still in it's infancy. Makink an individual mask (1 for each part number times the number of layers needed for the transistors and their interconnections). Their first yields were not that good. as they learned more and used better equipment, they improved and costs started to go down. Somewhere around 1978 the LSI (Large Scale Integration) chips began to standardize and the were able to change packaging. The silver was no longer needed as they used a metal
>  framework that was similar in design to the silver's design, but then they were able to cover it in ceramic and later plastic. The pins were made into the framework, thus saving on cost for the gold and tooling and masks.
> As for the metal bar used as a heatsink, the reason it gets hot is that it is drawing the heat away from the chip. The units made by Astrocade never had any heat sinks unless they were in the original batch from Bally. And they actually worked better. There were some improvements in the supporting circuitry to make the heat slightly less.
> As far as the bar, it should be fine to use, as long as the bottom air vents don't blocked. The whole system is called a "chimney effect" type of cooling. The topmost area will have the most heat because heat rises. As that happens, it creates a vacuum underneath it, so it draws in the cooler air from the bottom.
> Any Questions????
>
> From the only guy that is currently repairing Bally/Astrocade units.

12955:
Very nice!  But - you need to set the system Stack Pointer first!!
It's starting at $0000 and counts back $0010 every time it crashes
until it finds RAM at $5000 in the MESS emulator (also Astrocade.)

Recommended is SYSRAM, BEGRAM, or MUZPC as all are location $4FCE
and will not PUSH far enough to hit your MSTACK way down at $4F12.

Not needed is "LD  A,$00", "OUT  ($16),A" to clear the Master Osc.
Just move the EMUSIC up before the ACTINT to zero ALL Music Ports.

BTW "XOR A" loads A with 0 saving one byte, not that that's needed
and TABs ruin the alignment of your listing, use 8 SPACEs instead.


RCD

12971:
zhuowei_applications@yahoo.com wrote:
>>
if you replace the ROM files
of Robby Roto in MAME with an Astrocade BIOS and cartridge, the arcade
emulation will boot up into [low-res] consumer mode and display the standard
Astrocade menu.
>>

So, you're saying that you can boot up an arcade unit into low-res mode.  Sure.  There's no reason that you can't do that.  The screen-RAM would just map at $4000-$4FFF (instead of $4000-$7FFF as the normal hi-res mode would map).  The Bally's On-board ROM would have to be placed starting at $0000.  Since MAME allows you to map the keyboard, you should still be able to choose an option from the menu if you set up the keyboard mapping correctly.

You could also place an Astrocade cart in a specially created MAME "ROM" source file.  The special "ROM" would have the Astrocade on-board ROM at $0000 and then the Astrocade "cart" would be in the same assembly file with an ORG of $2000.

I guess this isn't really news to anyone, but I don't recall this topic popping up before, and I quite like it.  The nearest that this subject has come to being discussed before is booting an Astrocade into hi-res mode, which would be an achievement.  Booting an arcade machine into low-res mode is mentioned in the Nutting manual, and I guess it's not been put forward before because there hasn't been any reason to do it.

The most interesting reason to boot an arcade game like Wizard of Wor into low-res mode would be to run the on-board menu with an included cartridge.

To really mess things up, why not boot a hi-res game into low-res mode and see how much confusion that you can cause.  Try it with Wizard of Wor.  Here's the source code (which, honestly, I've never assembled myself before):

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/WOW_Latest_working_copy_of_full_disassembly_022104.asm

In the above source, search for this:

    ld     a,$01
L0006:    out     ($08),a    ; Set Video to HI-RES

Change it to this:

        XOR     A
L0006:    out     ($08),a    ; Set Video to CONSUMER MODE

Now all Hell should break loose when the game is run...  FUN!

Adam

Gunfight -- which is a home version of the Midway arcade game Gun Fight...leaving out the space makes the game run cooler -- is for two players only, but shows off some of the versatility of the Astrocade's controller. 12998:
Paul comes up with some pretty long names while archiving Bally tapes.  I've run into problems before, and found workarounds for these long filenames, but this time nothing I did allowed me to access the file on my own hard drive.  Some other folks on here archive too, so I thought that this information might prove useful.

Including my path, Paul named one of the files from Ken Lill's collection, this:

H:\Astrocade\_To_Upload\tape_backups (RAW Recordings by Paul Thacker)\Ken Lill\Box G\Mastermind(INPUT 257),Plastic Puzzle(514),Loan Repayment(768),King Hamurabi(1028),2000 AD(3D)(1285),Othello(1542),Artil Battle(1799),Sub Search(2056),Connect 4(2313) (raw, 300 baud).wav

I couldn't copy, move or delete this file because the name is too long.  Why Windows ALLOWS names and paths of this length to be created is beyond me.  Rrr.  The name freaks out Windows Explorer and even TeraCopy (a third-party file copier that allows longer paths and names).  In case this ever happens to you, here's what I did to fix it:

1) Mapped "H:\Astrocade\_To_Upload\tape_backups (RAW Recordings by Paul Thacker)\Ken Lill\Box G\" as network drive z: (any letter not in use, of course, will work).

2) Copied the file from z: to C:\

3) Renamed the file on c: to a shorter name, and then made a note of it with the actual name in a text file with the same shorter name.

4) I still couldn't remove the file from my local hard drive.  So I found these directions and did this:

http://superuser.com/questions/45697/how-to-delete-a-file-in-windows-with-a-too-long-filename

Once I figured this out, it wasn't hard to do, but I was getting pretty frustrated until that simple fix.  Which is only simple once you know how to do it.

Apparently this trouble can affect all versions of Windows.  I'm curious, would Linux or Mac users run into a problem like this?

Adam
